question: A commercial tenant bolts custom display shelving to the wall of a rented retail space for use in its business. Under which doctrine may the tenant remove the shelving before the lease ends?
choice_a: The trade fixture doctrine, which allows a commercial tenant to remove items installed for business purposes, provided the tenant repairs any resulting damage
choice_b: The doctrine of emblements, which applies only to cultivated crops
choice_c: Adverse possession, since the tenant has used the space exclusively
choice_d: The item automatically becomes the landlord's real property and may never be removed
explanation: Trade fixtures installed by a commercial tenant for conducting business remain the tenant's personal property and may be removed before the lease expires, so long as the tenant restores any damage caused by removal. This is an exception to the general rule that attached items become part of the real property.
source_note: national real property law - trade fixture doctrine

question: In determining whether an item attached to real property has become a fixture (and therefore transfers with the land), which factors do courts traditionally examine?
choice_a: Only the purchase price of the item
choice_b: The method of attachment, the item's adaptation to the property's use, and the intention of the party who installed it
choice_c: Only whether the item can be unplugged from an electrical outlet
choice_d: Only which party currently possesses the item
explanation: The traditional legal test for a fixture weighs the method/permanence of annexation, the item's adaptation to the use of the real property, and the intent of the annexor. Cost and unplugging ease are not controlling factors.
source_note: national real property law - fixture test

question: A tenant farmer plants and cultivates an annual crop of corn under a lease that expires before harvest. Under the doctrine of emblements, how is the crop treated?
choice_a: As real property that automatically transfers to the landlord upon lease expiration
choice_b: As a fixture that must remain attached to the land
choice_c: As personal property, and the tenant generally retains the right to enter and harvest it even after the tenancy ends
choice_d: As abandoned property belonging to whoever harvests it first
explanation: Emblements are cultivated, annual crops produced through a tenant's labor. They are classified as personal property, and the doctrine of emblements protects the tenant's right to re-enter and harvest crops planted during the tenancy even if the tenancy ends before harvest.
source_note: national real property law - doctrine of emblements

question: Which type of deed gives the grantee the greatest protection because the grantor warrants title against defects arising both during the grantor's ownership and during all prior periods of ownership?
choice_a: Special warranty deed
choice_b: Quitclaim deed
choice_c: Bargain and sale deed
explanation: A general warranty deed contains covenants warranting title against defects existing at any time in the chain of title, including before the grantor owned the property, offering the broadest protection to the grantee.
source_note: national real property law - deed types

question: A grantor conveys property by a deed in which they warrant title only against defects or claims arising during their own period of ownership, not against defects that existed before they acquired title. Which deed type is this?
choice_a: Special warranty deed
choice_b: General warranty deed
choice_c: Quitclaim deed
explanation: A special (limited) warranty deed limits the grantor's warranty to defects that arose only while the grantor held title, unlike a general warranty deed which covers the entire chain of title.
source_note: national real property law - deed types

question: A deed conveys 'whatever interest the grantor may have' in a property, with no warranties of title at all, and is commonly used to clear a cloud on title. What type of deed is this?
choice_a: General warranty deed
choice_b: Quitclaim deed
choice_c: Special warranty deed
explanation: A quitclaim deed conveys only whatever interest the grantor currently holds, if any, with no warranties of title. It is frequently used to release a potential claim or clear a title defect.
source_note: national real property law - deed types

question: Which of the following is required for a deed to be legally valid and effective between grantor and grantee?
choice_a: Recording the deed in the county land records
choice_b: Notarization by a licensed real estate broker
choice_c: A legal description of the property, the grantor's signature, and delivery of the deed to (and acceptance by) the grantee
choice_d: Payment of a stated minimum dollar amount of consideration
explanation: A deed must contain a legal description, be signed by a competent grantor, and be delivered to and accepted by the grantee to be valid. Recording is not required for validity between the parties -- it primarily establishes priority and public notice against later claimants.
source_note: national real property law - deed requirements

question: A metes and bounds legal description identifies a parcel's boundaries using a series of distances and directions (courses) that must ultimately return to which point?
choice_a: The nearest permanent benchmark
choice_b: The section corner
choice_c: The principal meridian
explanation: A metes and bounds description starts at a defined point of beginning, traces a sequence of courses (directions and distances) around the parcel's perimeter, and must close by returning exactly to the point of beginning.
source_note: national real property law - metes and bounds legal description

question: The 'lot and block' method of legal description identifies a parcel by referring to which of the following?
choice_a: A recorded subdivision plat map that assigns each parcel a lot number within a numbered block
choice_b: A series of compass bearings and distances beginning at a point of beginning
choice_c: Township, range, and section numbers from the government survey grid
choice_d: The property's street address as shown on a utility bill
explanation: The lot and block (recorded plat) system references a subdivision plat that has been surveyed and recorded in the public records, identifying each parcel by its lot number within a numbered block on that plat.
source_note: national real property law - lot and block legal description

question: Under the government (rectangular) survey system, a standard township is a square measuring approximately how large, and how many sections does it contain?
choice_a: 1 mile by 1 mile, containing 4 sections of approximately 160 acres each
choice_b: 6 miles by 6 miles, containing 36 sections of approximately 640 acres each
choice_c: 10 miles by 10 miles, containing 100 sections of approximately 320 acres each
choice_d: 36 miles by 36 miles, containing 6 sections of approximately 6,400 acres each
explanation: A township under the rectangular (government) survey system is a 6-mile by 6-mile square divided into 36 sections, each approximately one square mile, or about 640 acres.
source_note: national real property law - government rectangular survey system

question: A standard section of land contains 640 acres. How many acres are in the NE 1/4 of the SW 1/4 of that section?
choice_a: 160 acres
choice_b: 80 acres
choice_c: 40 acres
explanation: The SW 1/4 of a 640-acre section is 160 acres. The NE 1/4 of that 160-acre parcel is 40 acres (640 divided by 4, then divided by 4 again: 640 / 4 / 4 = 40).
source_note: national real property law - government survey land measurement

question: In the government rectangular survey system, the primary north-south reference lines are called ___, and the primary east-west reference lines are called ___.
choice_a: base lines; principal meridians
choice_b: ranges; townships
choice_c: townships; ranges
explanation: Principal meridians run north-south and base lines run east-west; together they form the reference grid from which townships (north-south rows called ranges, measured east-west, and tiers, measured north-south) are located.
source_note: national real property law - government rectangular survey system

question: When an appraiser or agent measures a house to calculate its gross living area, which space is properly included?
choice_a: Finished, heated, habitable square footage located above grade
choice_b: The unfinished basement, whether or not it is heated
choice_c: An attached garage used for vehicle storage
explanation: Gross living area (GLA) is generally defined as finished, heated, above-grade living space. Unfinished basements, garages, and unheated porches are typically measured and reported separately, not included in GLA.
source_note: national appraisal/measurement standards - gross living area

question: One acre of land contains how many square feet?
choice_a: 36,000 square feet
choice_b: 43,560 square feet
choice_c: 40,000 square feet
explanation: By definition, one acre equals 43,560 square feet, a standard unit of land measurement used nationally.
source_note: national land measurement standard

question: A county property tax lien attaches only to the specific parcel on which the tax is owed, while a recorded money judgment against an individual typically attaches to all real property that person owns within the jurisdiction. This distinguishes a ___ lien from a ___ lien.
choice_a: general; specific
choice_b: voluntary; involuntary
choice_c: specific; general
explanation: A specific lien attaches to one particular property (such as a property tax lien or a mortgage), while a general lien (such as a judgment lien) attaches to all property, real and sometimes personal, owned by the debtor in that jurisdiction.
source_note: national real property law - liens

question: A contractor who performs unpaid work on a property files a mechanic's lien. The lien's priority is typically determined by relating back to which date?
choice_a: The date the lien document was recorded
choice_b: The date the contract was signed
choice_c: The date the work was completed
choice_d: The date the work began or materials were first furnished on the project
explanation: Most jurisdictions give a mechanic's lien priority as of the date labor or materials were first furnished to the project, even though the lien itself is recorded later, which can place it ahead of liens recorded (but not furnished) earlier.
source_note: national real property law - mechanic's liens

question: An easement that benefits a specific parcel of land (the dominant estate) and automatically transfers with that land whenever it is sold is known as an easement...
choice_a: appurtenant
choice_b: in gross
choice_c: by license
explanation: An easement appurtenant benefits a dominant estate and burdens a servient estate; it runs with the land and transfers automatically with the dominant parcel. An easement in gross, by contrast, benefits a person or entity rather than a parcel of land.
source_note: national real property law - easements

question: A parcel of land is completely landlocked, with no legal access to a public road except across a neighboring parcel. A court may grant the landlocked owner which type of easement?
choice_a: An easement in gross
choice_b: An easement by necessity
choice_c: A license
explanation: An easement by necessity is created by law when a parcel has no legal access to a public road, giving the landlocked owner the right to cross an adjoining parcel that was once part of the same original tract.
source_note: national real property law - easement by necessity

question: A property owner tells a neighbor they may park in the owner's driveway whenever asked, and either party can end the arrangement at any time. This privilege is best classified as a...
choice_a: easement appurtenant that runs with the land
choice_b: easement in gross that survives a sale of the property
choice_c: license -- a personal, revocable privilege to use land that does not create an interest in real property
explanation: A license is a personal, revocable permission to use another's land. Unlike an easement, it does not create a permanent interest in real property and generally terminates when either party revokes it or when the licensor sells the property.
source_note: national real property law - licenses vs. easements

question: A survey reveals that a homeowner's fence extends two feet onto the neighboring lot. This situation is an example of a(n)...
choice_a: easement
choice_b: deed restriction
choice_c: riparian right
explanation: An encroachment occurs when a structure or improvement unlawfully extends onto an adjoining owner's land, as opposed to an easement, which is a legally granted right to use another's land.
source_note: national real property law - encroachments

question: To acquire title to land through adverse possession, a claimant's possession must generally be...
choice_a: actual, open and notorious, continuous for the statutory period, and hostile to the true owner's title
choice_b: secret, brief, and with the true owner's permission
choice_c: based solely on paying property taxes for one year
choice_d: established the moment the claimant first enters the land
explanation: Adverse possession generally requires possession that is actual, open and notorious (visible), continuous for the statutory period, hostile (without the owner's permission), and in most states exclusive.
source_note: national real property law - adverse possession

question: A lease has no fixed end date and automatically renews for successive equal periods, such as month-to-month, until either party gives proper notice to terminate. This is a(n)...
choice_a: estate for years
choice_b: periodic tenancy (estate from period to period)
choice_c: tenancy at will
explanation: A periodic tenancy automatically renews for successive, equal periods (e.g., month-to-month or year-to-year) until proper notice of termination is given, distinguishing it from an estate for years, which has a definite start and end date.
source_note: national real property law - leasehold estates

question: A tenant's lease has expired, but the tenant remains in possession of the property without the landlord's consent. This type of leasehold is called a...
choice_a: tenancy at will
choice_b: estate for years
choice_c: tenancy at sufferance
explanation: A tenancy at sufferance arises when a tenant who lawfully entered the property remains in possession after the lease term ends without the landlord's consent, technically making the tenant a holdover rather than a trespasser.
source_note: national real property law - leasehold estates

question: A landowner sells the surface rights to a parcel but retains all subsurface mineral rights. This transaction creates what result?
choice_a: An easement in gross benefiting the mineral owner
choice_b: A life estate in the minerals
choice_c: Automatic termination of the mineral rights after five years
choice_d: A severance of the mineral estate from the surface estate, creating two separately owned interests in the same land
explanation: Mineral rights can be severed from surface rights, creating two distinct, separately transferable estates in the same land -- a surface estate and a mineral estate.
source_note: national real property law - mineral rights severance

question: Water rights belonging to an owner of land bordering a non-flowing body of water such as a lake or ocean are called ___ rights, while rights belonging to land bordering a flowing waterway such as a river are called ___ rights.
choice_a: littoral; riparian
choice_b: riparian; littoral
choice_c: appropriative; littoral
explanation: Littoral rights apply to land bordering non-flowing bodies of water such as lakes, seas, and oceans, while riparian rights apply to land bordering flowing waterways such as rivers and streams.
source_note: national real property law - water rights

question: Which statement about air rights is correct?
choice_a: Air rights cannot legally be separated from surface ownership under any circumstances
choice_b: Air rights above a parcel can be sold, leased, or transferred separately from the surface, such as through a transfer of development rights
choice_c: Air rights automatically expire after 25 years regardless of use
choice_d: Air rights are considered personal property, not real property
explanation: Air rights are a real property interest that can be severed from the surface estate and conveyed or leased separately, as is commonly done in dense urban areas through transferable development rights.
source_note: national real property law - air rights

question: Two people hold title to a property as tenants in common. Which statement correctly describes this form of co-ownership?
choice_a: Both owners must hold exactly equal shares, and the interest automatically passes to the surviving co-owner at death
choice_b: The property cannot be sold unless both owners die simultaneously
choice_c: Each owner may hold an unequal percentage interest, and upon an owner's death, that owner's interest passes to their heirs or as directed by will, not automatically to the surviving co-owner
choice_d: Only married couples may hold title as tenants in common
explanation: Tenants in common may hold unequal, undivided interests in the property, and there is no right of survivorship -- each owner's interest passes through their estate upon death, unlike joint tenancy.
source_note: national real property law - tenancy in common

question: Creation of a valid joint tenancy with right of survivorship traditionally requires the 'four unities' of...
choice_a: price, location, size, and use
choice_b: marriage, kinship, residence, and citizenship
choice_c: recording, notarization, delivery, and acceptance
explanation: Traditional common law requires the four unities of time (interests acquired at the same time), title (via the same document), interest (equal shares), and possession (equal right to possess the whole) to create a joint tenancy.
source_note: national real property law - joint tenancy

question: Tenancy by the entirety is a form of co-ownership available only to which parties?
choice_a: Married couples, providing right of survivorship and, in many states, protection from the creditors of only one spouse
choice_b: Any two unrelated business partners
choice_c: Parent and adult child co-owners
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety is a special form of joint ownership recognized in many states exclusively for married couples, offering right of survivorship and, in many jurisdictions, protection of the property from the individual debts of just one spouse.
source_note: national real property law - tenancy by the entirety

question: In a condominium, an individual owner holds fee simple title to which of the following?
choice_a: Shares of stock in a corporation that owns the entire building
choice_b: The individual unit interior, along with an undivided percentage interest as a tenant in common in the building's common elements
choice_c: A leasehold interest only, renewable annually
choice_d: The entire building and all other units
explanation: Condominium ownership combines fee simple title to the individual unit with an undivided tenancy-in-common interest in the building's common elements (hallways, roof, land, amenities, etc.).
source_note: national real property law - condominium ownership

question: In a housing cooperative, a resident typically owns which of the following?
choice_a: Fee simple title to the specific unit occupied
choice_b: A tenancy-in-common interest in just that one unit
choice_c: Shares of stock in the corporation that owns the building, plus a proprietary lease granting the right to occupy a specific unit
choice_d: A recorded condominium deed to the unit
explanation: Cooperative ('co-op') ownership differs from condominium ownership: the resident owns shares in the corporation that holds title to the entire building, and occupies a specific unit under a proprietary lease rather than owning real property directly.
source_note: national real property law - cooperative ownership

question: A deed conveys property 'to Maria for life, then to Tom.' What interest does Tom hold, and what happens to Maria's rights at her death?
choice_a: Tom holds a reversion that returns the property to the original grantor
choice_b: Maria's interest passes to her own heirs regardless of Tom's interest
choice_c: Tom immediately holds fee simple title while Maria is still alive
choice_d: Tom holds a remainder interest that becomes possessory automatically upon Maria's death; Maria's right to possess and use the property ends at her death
explanation: Maria holds a life estate, which entitles her to possess and use the property only during her lifetime. Tom holds a remainder interest, which automatically becomes a possessory fee simple estate upon Maria's death, with no further conveyance required.
source_note: national real property law - life estates and remainders

question: A life estate is granted 'to Sam for the life of his mother, Ellen.' Sam's interest lasts as long as Ellen is alive, not as long as Sam is alive. This type of life estate is called a life estate...
choice_a: pur autre vie
choice_b: in remainder
choice_c: in reversion
explanation: A life estate pur autre vie ('for the life of another') is measured by the lifespan of someone other than the life tenant -- here, Ellen's life rather than Sam's.
source_note: national real property law - life estate pur autre vie

question: When a single individual (or a single entity) holds sole title to real property with no co-owners, that form of ownership is called ownership in...
choice_a: common
choice_b: severalty
choice_c: entirety
explanation: Ownership 'in severalty' means the property is held solely by one owner, whether an individual or a single legal entity, severed from any co-ownership.
source_note: national real property law - severalty ownership

question: A property is placed into a trust for estate-planning purposes. Which party holds legal title and manages the property for the benefit of another under the arrangement?
choice_a: The beneficiary
choice_b: The trustor (settlor)
choice_c: The trustee
explanation: In a trust, the trustor (or settlor) creates the trust and transfers property into it, the trustee holds legal title and manages the property according to the trust's terms, and the beneficiary receives the benefit of the trust property.
source_note: national real property law - trust ownership roles

question: A real estate investor purchases rental property in the name of a limited liability company (LLC) rather than in their own individual name. What is the primary ownership advantage of this approach?
choice_a: It automatically exempts the property from all property taxes
choice_b: It guarantees the property cannot be sold without unanimous shareholder consent
choice_c: It converts the property into a life estate
choice_d: It generally limits the owner's personal liability for claims arising from the property to the amount invested in the entity
explanation: Holding real estate through an LLC or similar business entity generally shields the individual owner's personal assets from liabilities connected to the property, limiting exposure to the amount invested in the entity, unlike direct individual ownership.
source_note: national real property law - business entity ownership

question: A property owner dies without a valid will (intestate) and without any surviving co-owner holding right of survivorship. How is title to the property typically transferred?
choice_a: Through a probate (or intestate succession) proceeding that distributes the property according to the state's intestacy laws
choice_b: The property automatically becomes owned by the state's real estate commission
choice_c: Title passes immediately and automatically to the deceased's closest neighbor
choice_d: The property cannot be transferred and remains permanently in the deceased's name
explanation: When an owner dies without a will, the property passes through probate under the state's intestate succession laws, which determine which heirs receive the property and in what shares.
source_note: national real property law - probate and intestate succession

question: A developer sells timeshare interests in a beachfront condominium unit, dividing the right to use the unit into one-week increments throughout the year among many purchasers. This ownership structure is known as a...
choice_a: tenancy in common with no time restrictions
choice_b: timeshare (interval ownership)
choice_c: life estate divided by calendar week
explanation: A timeshare (or interval ownership) divides use rights to a single unit among multiple purchasers, each holding the right to use the property for a specified recurring period, such as one week per year.
source_note: national real property law - timeshare ownership
